chunks: Muhammad, from Ahmad, from his father Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Halabi who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Can a slave be emancipated from among the oppressed (mustadh'afin)?' He said: 'Yes.'

key_terms.الرَّقَبَة: Raqabah — literally 'neck,' the legal term for a slave in classical Islamic jurisprudence; freeing a raqabah is prescribed as an act of expiation (kaffarah) in several Quranic injunctions
key_terms.الْمُسْتَضْعَفِين: Mustadh'afin — the oppressed, the weakened; those who have been rendered weak in faith, knowledge, or social power; in this jurisprudential context, refers to those who do not have clear religious conviction (neither fully Muslim nor explicitly polytheist)
key_terms.تُعْتَقُ: Yu'taqu — to be emancipated, freed from slavery

ai.seo_question: Can a slave from among the mustadh'afin (oppressed) be emancipated in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Al-Halabi asked Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) whether a slave could be freed from the category of mustadh'afin — those who are socially, economically, or spiritually oppressed and unable to distinguish the truth. The Imam affirmed this with a simple 'Yes,' establishing that the emancipation of a slave from the mustadh'afin fulfills the legal requirement for freeing a slave as an act of expiation or devotion. This ruling addresses the permissibility of emancipating those who are weak in faith or social standing.

en.hubeali: Muhammad, from Ahmad, form his father Muhammad Bin Isa, from Ibn Muskan, from Al Halby who said,
‘I said to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, ‘The (freeing of) a neck can be an emancipation from the oppressed?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Yes’.
